t: How To Handle An Out-Of-Control Student
q: So you have this student who seems determined to ruin your school year.

He is one of those rare students who has gotten a peek behind the curtain and has discovered that no matter what he does, within fifteen minutes or so he’ll be right back out on the playground or in your classroom doing as he wishes.
He knows your hands are tied. He knows you’ve tried everything. He knows he’s got you over a barrel.
You explain that his desk will be set apart until he can prove to you he can behave like a full-fledged, contributing member of the classroom.
Students like this need accountability, desperately. And down deep they know it. Their behavior screams out for it, craves it, pleads for it.
You may very well be the only person in his life in position to make such a heroic and potentially life-changing, life-saving stand.

t: How To Introduce Units Of Study And Set Your Students On Fire For Learning ur-students-on-fire-for-learning/
q: There exists an amazing strategy that will dramatically increase student interest, motivation, and comprehension in virtually whatever you’re studying.

The way it works is that instead of giving your students a preview of what they’re about to learn, instead of reading an introduction or teaching a more traditional first lesson . . . you will tell a story.
There once was a man named Howard Carter who spent six years searching for the lost tomb of a boy king.
Be careful not to get sidetracked writing out lists of facts or key points for your students.
Storytelling is the most flexible and dynamic medium available to teachers, and it will fit seamlessly into whatever standards or curriculum you’ve been asked to follow
